background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 36110/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that their case, which commenced in 1989 and terminated in 1996, was not heard within a reasonable time as required by the Convention. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 15 May 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The Turkish Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions.

In September 1980 the applicants were taken into police custody and were subsequently placed in detention on remand on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. In September 1988 the Erzincan Martial Law Court acquitted the applicants of the charges against them. In March, April and June 1989 the applicants brought individual actions before the Sinop Assize Court against the Treasury, pursuant to Law no. 466. They requested compensation for their unjustified detention. The applicants appealed, arguing that the amount of compensation awarded was not sufficient. On 30 May 1996 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants’ appeal and upheld the judgment of the assize court.

background_knowledge: The case originated in two applications (nos. 43185/98 and 43186/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that the proceedings in which they were sued in respect of property in Florida were not dealt with within a reasonable time. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 3 September 2002 the Court declared the applications partly admissible, having in the meantime joined them on 28 November 2000. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1)

The applicants, together with Dr Price’s wife, were sued by “K’, a former patient of Dr Price, in respect of property in Florida. The writ was issued on 12 February 1986. Before the action came to trial, the plaintiff was adjudicated bankrupt on 9 August 1989 and the trustee in bankruptcy continued the action. The trial was set down to commence in August 1994 but was postponed until the end of September 1994 because the judge was not available for the length of time needed for the hearing. The judge found that the transfer of the Florida property should be set aside on the ground that the defendants had not been able to rebut the presumption of undue influence.

The Court of Appeal confirmed the decision of the trial judge that the sum should be repaid, but that no interest should be paid on it. Dr Price had had possession of the properties and receipt of the rents since the completion of the sale, subject only to the agreement to allow [K] to use number 212 in the early months. On 30 March 1998 the applicants and Mrs Price were refused leave to appeal by the House of Lords. Lord Justice Nourse regarded this as a “rough and ready result”, but one which would “reduce the opportunities for further dispute between the parties”. On 19 April 1997 the applicants were refused. leave by the Court of. Appeal to appeal to the House Of Lords.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 42552/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mr H.Ç. Akbulut, a lawyer practising in Izmir. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. On 21 March 2002 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

The applicants were born in 1975 and 1970 respectively. They were taken into custody by police officers from the Anti-Terrorism Department of the Aydın Security Directorate on suspicion of their membership to an illegal organisation, namely the DHKP/C. In their police statements the applicants accepted the accusations against them. On 25 March 1997 the Izmir State Security Court, composed of two civilian judges and a military judge, convicted the applicants as charged and sentenced the first applicant to three years and nine months’ imprisonment. On 12 November 1997 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants’ appeal. Neither the applicants nor their lawyers were present in this last hearing. The decision, which was pronounced in the absence of the applicants and their lawyers, was deposited with the Registry of the IzMir State Security court on 21 November 1997.

The applicant was born in 1987 and is detained in Lublin. In 2006 he was convicted of three counts of battery and robbery and received prison sentences ranging from two to four years. The commission held that the applicant had been the leader of or an active participant in a planned collective remonstrance. The Lublin Regional Court dismissed the appeal on 4 April 2011. The court referred to the reasons given in the decision of 5 Nov 2010, holding that the decision had been lawful and justified.

On 28 April 2011 the Lublin Remand Centre Penitentiary Commission revoked its decision to classify the applicant as a ‘dangerous detainee’. It considered that the applicant’s behaviour had improved and that he no longer posed a threat to the security of the remand centre. in the case, holding that no offence had been committed. The case was settled out of court and the applicant was released without charge. In the case of the applicant, the judge ruled that he had not committed an offence and that the case should not be re-opened. He was released on bail and returned to Lublin prison.

The applicant was born in 1964 and is currently serving a sentence of imprisonment in HM Prison Craiginches, Aberdeen. The applicant was arrested on a charge of attempted murder arising out of a high speed car chase which occurred in the early hours of 29 October 1995. On 31 October 1995, the applicant appeared in court in respect of the various road traffic offences and the attempted murder of a police officer. The appeal was discontinued due to lack of court time and pressure of other business.

The High Court held that the failure to hear the evidence of W. resulted in unfairness and that further evidence should be heard. On 16 October 1998, W. gave evidence. The appeal was relisted for hearing on 8 January 1999 but the applicant's solicitors wrote to the court requesting that another date, possibly in the following week, be fixed due to the unavailability of counsel. On 24 June 1999, the appeal was heard before the High Court. The judgment of the court was given by the Lord Justice General, Lord Rodger, on 22 July 1999. It dismissed the applicant’s appeal. In his note of 20 November 1998, Lord Philip gave his view of the credibility and reliability of W., who gave evidence in the case.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 36705/97) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had prevented him from having access to his home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 8 June 1999 the Court declared the application not to be valid. The case was decided by the European Court of Human rights (ECHR) and the Government of Cyprus (GOC). The decision was made on the basis of the merits of the application.

The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Nicosia. He claimed that until July 1974 he used to live with his family in a house belonging to his parents in Lapithos, a village in the District of Kyrenia. In July 1974, as the Turkish army was advancing, the applicant and his family had been forced to leave. Ever since, they have not been able to return to the applicant’s parents’ house. The applicant produced the relevant affirmations of ownership issued by the Republic of Cyprus. According to these documents, the properties could be described as follows: (a) plot no. 288/3, sheet/plan 11/14 E.1, plot of land – olive grove, area 2,282 sq. m.

The applicant alleged that the Turkish occupation of northern Cyprus had prevented him from using and/or enjoying his properties. On this property had been constructed: a ground storey residence of an area of 152.25 sq. m; two shops of a area of 56 sq.m; two semidetached ground-storey residences (areas: 152. 25 sq.M and 63 sq. M respectively); one residence of a. area of 219.41sq. m. The applicant also had the right to use a freshwater spring. The application was denied by the Supreme Court of Cyprus and the appeal was dismissed on a technicality.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 36619/03) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the administrative proceedings to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Swedish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr M. Falk, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The case was decided on 29 November 2005 and the decision was made by the Court of Appeal.

The applicant was born in 1947 and lives in Orsa. The Tax Authority (skattemyndigheten) of the County of Kopparberg sent a preliminary consideration (övervägande) to the applicant informing him that it was considering disallowing the deduction he had made for the interest he had paid on debts in the amount of 2,000,000 Swedish kronor (SEK) He claimed that the transactions had taken place and that his tax return should be approved. On 27 September 1996 the Tax Authority decided to follow its preliminary consideration. With regard to the imposition of tax surcharges, it found that the applicant had submitted incorrect information about the purported transactions.

The applicant sued the Swedish State, through the Chancellor of Justice, before the District Court (tingsrätten) in Stockholm. He sought SEK 6,850,000 (approximately EUR 736,000) in damages on the grounds that the Tax Authority and the administrative courts had not afforded him a fair procedure. He invoked national legislation as well as the Convention and its case-law. The State contested the suit, claiming that it had not caused the applicant any injury, either by fault or neglect, for which he could claim damages. The District Court rejected the applicant’s claims. The applicant appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal, maintaining his claims. On 11 September 2003 the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal.

On 2 November 2005 the Court of Appeal upheld the lower court’s judgment in full. With regard to the complaint about the length of the proceedings, the court, without giving any reasons, found that the tax proceedings could not be considered to have been of excessive duration. On 12 October 2005 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) where the case is still pending, awaiting a decision on leave to appeal. The case is currently awaiting a Decision on Leave to appeal by the Supreme Supreme Court of Sweden, which is expected to take place within the next few months. The applicant has appealed the decision to the Court of Appeal.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 19365/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, serving a sentence of mandatory life imprisonment, alleged that the Parole Board did not provide the guarantees and procedures required by Article 5 § 4 when examining whether he should be released. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared the remainder of application admissible in a decision of 23 September 2003. The Government replied to the applicant's observations on just satisfaction and the Court ruled in favour of the Government.

The applicant was born in 1959 and is serving a sentence of life imprisonment in HM Prison Doncaster. He was convicted in or around 1981 for the murder of an acquaintance. The Parole Board recommended that the applicant should be transferred to open conditions, and that his detention should be reviewed after two years. By letter dated 6 July 2001 the Secretary of State informed the Prison Service that he did not accept the Parole board's recommendation for transfer. The applicant's first hearing under new arrangements was scheduled for November 2003. At the applicant's request, it was deferred until May 2004 to allow the applicant time to complete certain courses identified in the reports.

The Court declared the remainder of application admissible. In June 2001 the applicant was transferred to HM Prison Manchester. He claimed that he did not receive notification of the parole decision until sometime after 13 September 2001. The applicant stated that he wanted to seek judicial review of the decision, but was unable to find a solicitor who was prepared to act on his behalf. His then solicitors gave advice that judicial review stood little prospect of success as the reports recommending a move to open conditions had been slightly ambiguous, there were a number of very unfavourable reports and the Secretary of State had given extensive reasons for rejecting the recommended move.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 38629/97) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated on account of the lack of an oral hearing before the Administrative Court of Appeal in proceedings concerning social security benefits. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. By a decision of 4 May 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section.

The applicant, who was born in 1919, applied for disability benefits under the Social Insurance Act (Lagen om allmän försäkring, 1962:381; hereinafter “the 1962 Act’) He claimed that he was in need of assistance and had additional costs due to a speech impediment caused by a laryngectomy operation in 1979. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Västmanland. On 13 November 1992 the court gave judgment in his favour. The court did not hold an oral hearing nor, apparently, did the applicant request one.

Insurance Board (Riksförsäkringsverket) appealed against the County Administrative Court’s judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in Stockholm. The Board claimed that the information in the case showed that, before the age of 65, the applicant had not suffered a functional impairment to such an extent that his need of assistance and extra expenses on account thereof had made him eligible for a disability allowance. The applicant made submissions in response to the Board's appeal. On 25 February 1993 he requested the Administrative court to hold an oral hearing during which the person in charge of the case at the Office should give evidence. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten). He requested that the case be referred back to the Administrative Court of Appeal for re-examination. background_knowledge: The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 18711/91) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 4 April 1991. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (Art. 6-3-c). The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the case of Maxwell v the United UK should be heard by the same Chamber (Rule 21 para. 6).

The Government submitted their written reply to the applicant’s claims for just satisfaction under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. On 15 April 1994 the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would not submit written observations in reply. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 18 April 1994. The Court heard addresses by Mr Loucaides, Lord Rodger and Ms Rae as well as replies to its questions. There appeared before the Court: Mr I. Christie, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Lord. Rodger of Earlsferry, QC, Lord Advocate, Mr R. Reed, Counsel and Ms A.M. Chisholm, Solicitor.

Three masked men carried out a robbery at a post office in Falkirk, Scotland, in the course of which they assaulted three post-office employees. Mr Boner and two other men were arrested and remanded in custody. The applicant received legal aid for the preparation of his defence and for his representation by counsel at the trial. During the trial a prosecution witness, Mrs G., entered the courtroom prior to giving evidence and spoke to one of the applicant’s co-accused, against whom charges had been dropped. When Mrs G. was called to give evidence, the applicant's counsel objected on the basis of her earlier presence in court. The trial judge adjourned the case and instructed prosecuting counsel to make further inquiries.

The jury found the applicant guilty on all the charges. Taking account of his numerous previous convictions, the judge sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. Mr Boner instructed new solicitors, who asked a different counsel to advise on the prospects of an appeal and to draft a note of appeal. In his opinion dated 10 June 1990 counsel stated his view that the only possible ground of appeal related to the “admissibility of the evidence of Mrs G.“ and to the question “that the trial judge erred in exercising discretion in allowing her to be present“. However, he conceded that he had not been provided with sufficient information to be able properly to base an opinion.

Scottish Legal Aid Board refused Mr Boner's application for legal aid in November 1990. Board added that it could not see any merit in the appeal. Despite the advice of his solicitors and counsel, MrBoner decided to proceed with the appeal and presented his own case on 24 January 1991 before the High Court of Justiciary. Appeal court considered the first two grounds of appeal relating to Mrs G. and held that these were ill-founded and that the trial judge had approached the matter properly. It did however examine other points raised by the applicant, but reached “the clear conclusion that there was no miscarriage of justice in the case’.

It originated in an application (no. 18711/91) against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 4 April 1991 by a British citizen. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations. The applicant, Mr Anthony Boner, is a British citizen born in 1960. He lives in Glasgow, Scotland. On 14 December 1989 three masked men, armed with a shotgun and a knife, carried out a robbery at a post office in Glen Village, Falkirk, Scotland, in the course of which they assaulted three post-office employees. Between 29 March and 10 April 1990 he stood trial in the High Court of Justiciary sitting in Edinburgh. The applicant received legal aid for the preparation of his defence. When Mrs G. was called to give evidence, the applicant’s counsel objected on the basis of her earlier presence in court. The trial judge adjourned the case and instructed prosecuting counsel to make further inquiries into the matter. The jury found the applicant guilty on all the charges. Taking account of his numerous previous convictions, the judge sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. The applicant, through his solicitor, lodged an intimation of intention to appeal against conviction. An application to extend legal aid to the appeal proceedings had been submitted in May 1990. Despite the advice of his solicitors and counsel, Mr Boner decided to proceed with the appeal. The applicant, who had no legal knowledge and had no assistance with his submissions, presented his own case on 24 January 1991 before the High Court of Justiciary. The Crown was represented by counsel. There is no indication in the record that the court required counsel for the Crown to address it. The court dismissed the first two grounds of appeal relating to Mrs G. and held that these were ill-founded and that the trial judge had approached the matter properly. It did however examine other points raised by the applicant, but reached “the clear conclusion that there was no miscarriage of justice in the case’. The appeal against conviction was unanimously dismissed. The case was heard at the High Court in London.

The applicant earned his living by cultivating this land. The Directorate General refused to submit the information or documents requested by the Gaziantep Administrative Court. The court held that the impugned decision of 11 May 2000 and the refusal of the decision to annul the right holder status of the applicant were unlawful.

The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 15 April 2002. The decision was served on the applicant on 5 July 2002. Directorate General to submit the relevant information and documents had been in accordance with the domestic legislation. The applicant appealed. The appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Administrative court on 15April 2002. This decision was serviceed on 5July 2002. It was decided that the application was not viable and that the applicant should not be allowed to appeal the decision. The application was dismissed and the applicant was not permitted to appeal. The case was settled out of court in April 2002 and the appeal was decided out of Court in April 2003.

Dauban of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. It was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1)

The applicant claims to have arrived in the United Kingdom at the age of three. There is no official record of his presence until 1994, when he was eight years old. Indefinite leave to remain was granted to the applicant, outside the immigration rules, on 1 December 2003. He was convicted on 21 February 2007 of two counts of possession of Class A drugs with intent to supply. He pleaded guilty on the basis that he had been coerced into letting his premises be used for the preparation and sale of drugs by a group of people whom he feared because of a previous attack in 2005. On 18 October 2007 he was notified of the Secretary of State’s intention to deport him.

The applicant appealed against the decision to deport him and his appeal was dismissed by the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal on 13 March 2008. The Tribunal noted the applicant’s previous criminal record: he had been convicted of possession of Class A and Class B drugs in February 2004. It was not accepted that he had family life in the United Kingdom. Whilst the applicant would have practical difficulties in relocating to Nigeria, he could re-establish his private life there. The tribunal took into account the case of Üner v the Netherlands [GC], no. 46410/99, ECHR 2006‑XII, in finding that, on balance, and having due regard to the public interest, the applicant's deportation was proportionate.

The applicant was taken into immigration detention on 10 November 2009 and directions for his deportation to Nigeria were set on 12 November 2009 for 19 November 2009. On 13 November 2009 the applicant sought interim measures from this Court under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court to prevent his deportation. He submitted with his application a report from a specialist psychiatric registrar dated 14 September 2009, which stated that the applicant had attempted suicide on 13 August 2009. The Government informed the Court that they had not previously been aware of the applicant’s attempted suicide, but had now considered the psychiatric report. The applicant did not renew his application for judicial review. He was described as suffering from moderate depression.

The applicant notified the authorities in the immigration detention centre that he had taken an overdose of paracetamol on 29 December 2009. He was assessed by the medical team and found only to have taken a few tablets. No further concerns as to his well-being appear to have been raised and the applicant was released from immigration detention on 13 January 2010. He does not claim to have made any further attempts at suicide. The Government therefore invited the Court to lift the interim measure which had been indicated in respect of the applicant. That there were sufficient mental health facilities in Nigeria, which would be available to the applicant if needed. The Acting President decided to prolong until further notice the interim measures under Rule 39.

The applicant was born in 1941 and is detained in Her Majesty’s Prison Durham. He broke into a family home, where he stabbed to death a man, his wife and their adult son. He then repeatedly raped their 18 year‑old daughter, having first dragged her past her father's body. At trial he pleaded not guilty, denying the killings and claiming that the sexual intercourse had been consensual. rewrited_text: The case originated in an application (no. 63131/00) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that a delay in releasing him from prison had given rise to a violation of Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The hearing before the Court of Appeal was scheduled for 12 April 2000 at 8.45 a.m. On that day the Cracow Court of appeal upheld the decision of the Regional Court. No further appeal lay against the decision. The governor of the Tarnów Mościce Prison ordered the applicant to be released on 14 April 2000 and served him with a copy of the Court's decision.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 1303/02) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. By a decision of 8 July 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was decided by the Court's Chamber on 9 July 2003. The decision was made by the Chief Justice of the European Court of Justice.

The applicant is a United Kingdom national, who was born in 1944 and is currently serving a sentence of imprisonment in HMP Maidstone. On 16 April 1997, the Chief Constable of South Wales authorised the installation of covert recording devices at the applicant's cottage. Over 160 hours of tapes were obtained between the period of 25 April to 9 June 1997, on which latter date the applicant and his wife were arrested. He was convicted of charges inter alia of conspiracy to import controlled drugs and possession of controlled drugs in connection with importation of marijuana and cocaine from overseas. A confiscation order was imposed on him on 24 September 1998 in the sum of 50,169.18 pounds sterling (GBP)

The case was heard in the U.S. Court of Appeal on 17 October 2000. It was the first time the case had been heard by a full court of appeal. The case was decided in favour of the defendant. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court of the United States. The appeal was dismissed on 18 October 2000, and the case was settled in court on 17 November 2000, with the decision being quashed by the Court of Appeals. The verdict was: "Not guilty of the charge of misconduct in public office. The jury was therefore unable to reach a verdict on the case." The case has been appealed and the decision was overturned.
rewrited_text: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant invoked Articles 8 and 13 in relation to the covert recording by the police of conversations in his cottage. At trial, the applicant's defence alleged that the recorded discussions, which occurred while he and the others concerned were under the influence of drugs, were “drug-crazed ramblings” The applicant was convicted of charges inter alia of conspiracy to import controlled drugs and possession of controlled drugs in connection with importation of marijuana and cocaine from overseas. He was sentenced to a total of fifteen years' imprisonment. A confiscation order was imposed on him on 24 September 1998 in the sum of 50,169.18 pounds sterling (GBP) The applicant's renewed application was refused by the Court of Appeal on 17 October 2000.

background_knowledge: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 19 February 1993. It originated in an application (no. 14220/88) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 2 July 1988. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (art, 6-1) The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs E. Palm, the elected judge of Swedish nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court.

Hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 October 1993. Court heard addresses by Ms Jagander, Mr Gaukur Jörundsson and Mr Ravnsborg. Registrar that the Delegate did not intend to file a memorial in reply. Commission produced a number of documents, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions, and the applicant submitted his claims under Article 50 (art. 50) The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court: Ms E. Jagander,. Ms C. Renfors, Legal Adviser, Ministry of Justice, Adviser.

Göran Ravnsborg, a university lecturer in law, is a Swedish citizen and lives in Lund in Sweden. He held a power of attorney from his adoptive mother, Mrs Karin Schieck, and, on 19 November 1982, he was appointed administrator (god man) for her friend, Mrs Marie Åkerblom. In 1987, while the above-mentioned proceedings were pending, the Board of the Principal Guardian (Överförmyndarnämnden - ‘the Board’) in Göteborg asked the District Court to appoint an administrator for Mrs Schiecks. The applicant, on his own and Mrs Siescheck’s behalf, filed a counter-claim and sought the immediate dismissal of the members of the Board.

The District Court, considering the applicant’s statements “improper“ within the meaning of Chapter 9, Article 5, of the Code of Judicial Procedure, ordered him, at a sitting on 18 May 1987, to pay a fine of 1,000 Swedish kronor. The applicant appealed from the above decision to the Court of Appeal for Western Sweden (Hovrätten för Västra Sverige). He asked for an oral hearing and complained of not having had the possibility to defend himself orally before the District Court. He expressed the opinion that the likelihood of his being granted leave to appeal was very small in view of the “generally lethargic’ attitude of the final instance’ June 1987 was the 30th anniversary of President Ronald Reagan's inauguration. Reagan was the first president to be inaugurated in the U.S. since George H.W. Bush in 1983. The ceremony was held at the White House in Washington, D.C. on June 8. The event was attended by then- Vice President George W. Bush. The White House was the second largest in the country at the time, with a population of 1.9 million. The U.N. was the largest in Europe, with 1.7 million people. The United States was the third-largest in the world, with 6.2 million people, followed by Germany.

On 2 July 1987 the applicant, on his own and Mrs Schieck’s behalf, lodged an appeal with the Court of Appeal. He asked that his case be heard by a specially composed District Court as he wished to have certain members disqualified from sitting. He alleged that one of its members had a “far-reaching tendentiously fascist way of presiding’ over the court and was “grossly partial in favour of municipal interests, collegiate corruption and abuse of public power through high-handedness, terror and reactionary principles’ On 4 November 1987, in a separate decision from the one mentioned in paragraph 13 above, the Court. of Appeal rejected the appeal.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 31721/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1978 and lives in İzmir. He was taken into police custody in October 2001 on suspicion of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, namely the PKK (Kurdistan Workers' Party) During his police custody, the applicant signed a form explaining arrested persons' rights, whereby he was reminded of his right to remain silent. The applicant admitted that he had aided and abetted the PKK and acted as courier for the organisation. On 20 June 2002 the Izmir State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to three years and nine months' imprisonment. In convicting the applicant, the court said that the applicant had acted as a PKK courier and helped him in certain illegal activities.

Izmir State Security Court relied on the applicant's police statement, which had been taken in the absence of a lawyer. The court further took into consideration the police statement of N.S. who had given evidence that the applicant had been involved in the activities of the PKK. On 10 October 2003 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It concluded that the. applicant'sPolice statement, in which he had admitted to his involvement in the PKK, had. been confirmed by other evidence in the case file. The applicant's appeal was dismissed on October 10, 2003, and he was sentenced to a year in prison.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 55853/00) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was represented before the Court by Mr Ulf Jacobson, a juris candidate practising in Stockholm. The Swedish Government (“the Government”) were represented by Mrs E. Jagander of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs as their Agent. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was lodged by a Swedish national, Mr Robert Edward Miller (‘the applicant’), on 9 April 1999.

The applicant was born in 1918 and lives in Stockholm. Until his retirement in March 1983 he worked as a teacher for 17 hours per week. He claimed that, even before his 65th birthday in 1983, he had incurred extra costs due to his illness, Charcot-Marie-Tooth0, from which he had suffered since the 1970's and which had been diagnosed in September 1982. In support of his claim, he submitted: A medical certificate dated 27 August 1996, produced by the applicant's general practitioner, Doctor P. Dekany, supporting his application for disability benefits. A statement dated 23 March 1983 by Mr P.K. Thomas, Professor and Doctor of the Royal Free Hospital School of Medicine, University of London.

Social Insurance Office (försäkringskassan -hereinafter ‘the Office’) of the County of Stockholm rejected the application, finding that the applicant's disability had not reached the level required under Chapter 9, section 2 before he turned 65 years of age. The applicant, represented by a lawyer, appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) and requested that an oral hearing be held in his case because he wished to call as witnesses his personal doctor, the doctor appointed by the Office and all the members of the Office who had participated in the decision of his case. On 15 January 1998 the County administrative court refused the request with reference to section 9 of the Administrative Court Procedure Act.

The applicant appealed against the lower court's judgment to the Stockholm Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) He requested the appellate court to find that he was entitled to disability benefits at a level corresponding to 36 % of the basic amount as of July 1994. He further requested that the court hold an oral hearing, on the same grounds as those he had presented to theLower Court. In response he reiterated his request for an Oral hearing, relying on Article 6 of the Convention. The Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten), observing that it did not normally hold oral hearings, rejected the applicant's request for a hearing and gave him three weeks within which to submit additional written observations.

Supreme Administrative Court refused him leave to appeal in February 2000. It said the County Administrative Court's refusal to hold a hearing was not deemed incompatible with the Convention. In this connection the applicant was given a copy of an analysis presented to the Supreme Administrative Court by its legal secretary, which included an opinion to the effect that the refusal of a hearing to be held was not considered incompatible with a Convention. On 29 February 2000 it refused him left to appeal, and he was not allowed to appeal against the decision. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, France, in March 2000, and the appeal was dismissed.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 47335/06) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1948 and lives in Bradford. He was employed by Serco Limited (“Serco”) from 5 December 2003 to his dismissal on 30 June 2004. Serco provided transport to local authorities, including Bradford City Council. The majority of his passengers were Asian in origin. There had been no complaints about his work or his conduct at work. His supervisor, who was of Asian origin, had nominated him for the award of “first-class employee”. On 15 June 2004 the applicant was elected as a local councillor for the BNP. After taking legal advice Serco summarily dismissed him.

The applicant lacked sufficient continuous service to bring an action for unfair dismissal. On 12 August 2004 he lodged a statutory claim of race discrimination in the Employment Tribunal pursuant to the Race Relations Act 1976 (“the 1976 Act’) The Employment Tribunal dismissed the claim of direct discrimination as it was satisfied that if any discrimination existed against the claimant it was not on racial grounds but rather on health and safety grounds. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Employment Appeal Tribunal. On 27 July 2005 his appeal was upheld on the ground that the Tribunal had erred in its construction of the phrase “on racial grounds” by failing to interpret its meaning broadly. Mummery LJ found the applicant’s submission that he had been subjected to direct race discrimination to be wrong in principle and inconsistent with the purposes of the legislation. In rejecting the claim of direct discrimination, the Court of Appeal noted that: “Mr Redfearn was treated less favourably not on the ground that he was white, but on the grounds of a particular non-racial characteristic shared by him with a tiny proportion of the white population’” The dividing line of colour or race was not made by Serco, but by the BNP which defines its own composition by colour and race. ‘ could not be applied to a person who was not of the same colour as Mr Redfearn,’ said the Court of Appeal. A more general and meaningful provision along similar lines would be one applying to membership of a political organisation like the BNP, which existed to promote views hostile to members of a different colour. ‘There is no respect in which the relevant provisions of the 1976 Act are incompatible with the Convention rights,” said the Appeal Court. The applicant was refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords. The case was heard at the High Court in London and the appeal was dismissed.

background_knowledge: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 24 November 1998. The Government accordingly appointed Sir Robert Carnwath to sit as an ad hoc judge. Mr G. Bonello, substitute judge, replaced Mr Türmen, who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case.

In 1987 the applicant, who was born in 1926, was convicted of manslaughter by the Central Criminal Court, London. The applicant was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. He was released in August 1988. On 2 January 1996 the applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of attempted rape of his next-door neighbour. He maintained that he had had sexual intercourse with the woman with her consent and the woman claimed that the incident had taken place after she had blacked out from drinking. background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 35615/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) Two Polish nationals, Mr Władysław Krzych and Mr Tadeusz Gurbierz (‘the applicants’), on 31 October 2003. In 1992 and 1993 the prosecutor conducted an investigation in connection with the applicants’ allegedly illegal business activities. On 16 December 1993 they were charged with fraud. On 28 September 2004 the trial court convicted the applicants but reduced the suspended prison terms to which they had been sentenced. They relied on the 2004 Act on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial.

The Gliwice Regional Court dismissed their appeal against the judgment of 28 September 2004. background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 62324/00) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 26 May 1999. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 1 December 2005 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. It was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the convention, it was decided that the application should be examined on the basis of its merits.

The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Kraków, Poland. On 14 January 1998 the applicant was arrested by the police. The court found that keeping the applicant in custody was justified by the strong suspicion that he had committed the offences, the probability that a severe sentence would be imposed and the fact that the third alleged perpetrator was still in hiding. The applicant appealed against those decisions arguing that there was no evidence that once released he would obstruct the proper course of the proceedings or abscond. The first decision was taken at a public hearing at which the applicant and his lawyers were present. The second decision was taking into consideration his difficult family situation as his parents needed his support.

In 1999 the trial court held in total thirteen hearings. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. On 13 April 2000 the Kraków Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, quashed the impugned judgment and remitted the case. The court further decided to prolong the applicant’s detention on remand. His lawyers were present at the hearing on 27 July 2000. The Regional Court prolonged the applicant's detention justifying it with reference to the reasonable suspicion that he had committed offences in question and the severity of the anticipated penalty. Nevertheless, the court decided to limit the period for which the detention was to be prolonged to 31 January 2001.

The applicant’s detention was further prolonged at public hearings held on 22 November 2000 and 20 April, 13 June, 27 September and 13 December 2001. It appears that on each occasion the Regional Court repeated the grounds for detention given previously: the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences and the severity of the penalty that might be imposed. The decisions were upheld on appeal by the Kraków Court of Appeal. On 3 June 2003 the Supreme Court partly allowed the cassation appeal, quashed the appeal court's judgment and remitted the case. The applicant was acquitted of the charge of attempted murder and his sentence was reduced to five years’ imprisonment.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 57592/08) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. On 6 October 2008, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal.

background_knowledge: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 11 September 1992. It originated in an application (no. 15058/89) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 2 December 1988. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30).

The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 April 1993. There appeared before the Court: Mrs Glover, Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr M. Baker, Q.C., Counsel, Mr G. Berry, Department of Health, Mr J. Evans, Trent Regional Health Authority, Advisers. The Court heard addresses by Mr Baker for the Government, by Mr Loucaides for the Commission and by Ms Hampson for the applicant, as well as replies to its questions. The Registrar received on 29 January 1993 the applicant's memorial and, on 1 February, the Government’s.

Dr Royce Darnell has been unemployed since the Trent Regional Health Authority terminated his employment as a consultant microbiologist and Director of the Public Health Laboratory in Derby. This case concerns the length of time that proceedings relating to this dismissal have taken. The applicant appealed to the Secretary of State against his dismissal on 23 May 1984. A professional committee was appointed in accordance with paragraph 190 of the Terms and Conditions of Service of Hospital Medical and Dental Staff. After holding a hearing on 14 May 1985, the professional committee reported to the secretary of state who, in September 1985, sought further information about the case. The application was dismissed on three months’ notice with effect from 19 August 1984.

Dr Darnell was dismissed by the Department of Health and Social Security in 1985. The RHA challenged the decision in the High Court. The Secretary of State directed the RHA to offer him a new post in the region without managerial responsibility. On 29 February 1988, having proceeded on the basis of the written material which included further written submissions, the Secretary of state decided to confirm the applicant’s dismissal. In November 1988, the second Industrial Tribunal hearing was cancelled as the applicant refused to accept such a compromise. The application for judicial review was dismissed on 3 November 1988. The applicant had also sought reinstatement, re-engagement and damages for dismissal by proceedings.

Dr Darnell lodged his application (no. 15058/89) with the Commission on 2 December 1988. He complained under Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention that the “civil rights’ proceedings taken against him which led to the final termination of his employment took an unreasonable length of time. He also alleged that the Secretary of State and the RHA had followed a procedure which was neither fair nor public and that the former was not independent or impartial. The Commission declared the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of the proceedings admissible and dismissed the remainder of his application.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 42735/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. In August 2003 the applicant turned 60 years of age. Prior to that date she was in receipt of long-term incapacity benefit. As a result, the applicant claimed that she was some GBP 24.04 per week worse off as a result of her transition from IB to State pension. She complained to the Department of Work and Pensions concerning the differential treatment but was informed that nothing could be done.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 68693/01) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the criminal charges against them had not been determined within a reasonable time within the meaning of Article 6. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 12 June 2003 the Court declared the application partly admissible.

On 20 October 1992 the first applicant was charged with offences against the Act on freshwater fish farms of 5 April 1989 (bekendtgørelse nr. 224), henceforth also called the 1989 Act. On 13 September 1993 an indictment was submitted to the City Court in Fjerritslev before which the trial was scheduled for 9 December 1993. The trial was adjourned awaiting the outcome of a corresponding pending criminal case, considered to be a ‘test-case’ The proceedings in the test-case were finally determined on appeal by a High Court judgment of 21 September 1995. By judgment of 28 May 1997 the applicant was convicted and sentenced to pay a fine of 68,000 Danish kroner.

The second applicant, as manager of two limited companies which each owned a freshwater fish farm, was charged with offences against the amended Act of 31 September 1994 on freshwater fish farms partly in conjunction with the former Act of 5 April 1989. The case was brought before the Supreme Court on 15 January 1999, where it was joined with the second applicant’s appeal (see below). II. The High Court of Western Denmark upheld the applicant's conviction, but increased the fine to DKK 95,000 and the amount to be confiscated toDKK 384,000. The applicant was granted permission to procure an expert witness, who during the preparation of the case was requested to reply in writing to specific questions formulated by counsel, and approved by the prosecutor.

A hearing was held on 24 February 1997 and the case was scheduled to commence on 8 September 1997. On 16 September 1997 the City Court in Mariager convicted the applicant and sentenced him to pay a fine of DKK 275,000. The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in London. He was arrested in London on suspicion of trafficking of illegal drugs. In his statements before the British police, the applicant maintained that he had been importing clothing goods from Turkey and had not been aware of the trafficking of drugs by his partners. The Crown Court acquitted the applicant of all charges and ordered his release in September 1998. The applicant is currently in detention on remand in the United Kingdom. In Turkey, he is accused of trafficking illegal drugs by establishing a criminal organisation pursuant to Article 403 of the former Criminal Code (Law no. 765). In that indictment the public prosecutor indicated the involvement of the applicant in the alleged acts, without bringing any charges against him.

On 15 July 1999 the military judge sitting on the İzmir State Security Court hearing the applicant’s case was replaced by a civilian judge. On 20 September 1999 the applicant went back to Turkey; he was placed in detention on remand the following day. At the subsequent hearing on 30 September 1999, the applicant submitted his statements before the court and denied his involvement in the trafficking of illegal drugs. On 27 March 2003, on the basis of the investigation conducted by the British authorities, the  applicant was found guilty as charged and sentenced to twenty four years’ imprisonment and a fine. On 31 March 2003 the applicant appealed against that judgment. On 4 March 2004 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment.

In June 2005, the applicant requested the reassessment of his case and the application of the more favourable clauses in the new Code. On 16 December 2005, after having examined the case file, the İzmir Assize Court reduced the applicant’s sentence to twenty years’ imprisonment and decreased the amount of the fine. On 3 July 2008 the applicant was sentenced to 20 years and ten months of imprisonment and a fine pursuant to Article 188 of the Criminal Code (Law no. 5237) On 9 April 2009 the Court of Cassation held a hearing and heard the submissions of the applicant's lawyer. Finally, the higher court upheld the judgment with a minor procedural correction.

A series of armed robberies was carried out by a number of armed males in Liverpool. The police were tasked with investigating, and arresting, any further members of the gang and recovering the money from the robberies. The information which came into their possession indicated that Dean De La Cruz had often given 19 New Henderson Street as his address. They knew that the robberies had involved the use of firearms. A search warrant was issued permitting a search of the premises for the cash. They were instructed to obtain forcible entry at 7 a.m. to coincide with the other searches. They experienced some difficulty as a previous tenant had had a hole in the door.

The noise of the battering ram awoke and frightened the applicants. Medical reports indicated that the applicants were suffering from varying degrees of post traumatic stress disorder. The applicants brought proceedings against the Chief Constable of Merseyside Police for the tort of maliciously procuring a search warrant, unlawful entry and false imprisonment. On 31 October 2002 the County Court Judge rejected the applicants’ claims. He found that the method of forcible entry was justified as the police had foremost in their minds the potential danger from the use of firearms by the suspect robber. He held that the entry was made subject to a lawful search warrant and also under the powers of section 17 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984. background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 36936/05) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The applicant alleged that the monitoring of his medical correspondence while he was in prison breached his right to respect for his correspondence and private life under Article 8 of the Convention. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the convention) The case was decided by the Court of Appeal on 7 February 2008 and the decision was made to allow the application to proceed. The application was made by Mr J. Scott, a lawyer practising at Langleys Solicitors.

In 2002 the applicant was held in a high-security prison which held Category A (high-risk) prisoners as well as Category B prisoners such as himself. He expressed his concerns about his medical correspondence with his external medical specialist being read and applied to the prison governor for a direction that such correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. It was decided that the applicant’s medical correspondence would not be read provided that certain conditions were met. All outgoing and incoming mail was to be marked “medical in confidence” Outgoing correspondence would be checked to ensure that it was being sent to a nominated address. Incoming correspondence was to have a distinctive stamp of the relevant health authority. The prison governor subsequently reconsidered his decision after seeking advice from HM Prison Service Headquarters.

The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the prisoner's request to be able to see his medical records. The Prison Service had argued that it would be difficult to allow the prisoner to see the medical records of other prisoners. The court ruled that the prisoner was entitled to the right to see a medical record of his medical history. The prisoner was allowed to keep his medical record, but the prison was not allowed to see it. The prison was ordered to pay the prisoner a fine of £1,000. The judge said that this was not enough to cover the cost of the prison and that the prison would have to pay a fee for the privilege.

The Court of Appeal concluded that the monitoring of the applicant’s medical correspondence was a proportionate interference with his Article 8 rights. It did not exclude the possibility that in another case it might be disproportionate to refuse confidentiality to medical correspondence in the prison context. It considered that although it was of course possible to verify the existence, address and qualifications of the applicants external medical specialist, there was no way of ensuring that the latter would not be intimidated or tricked into transmitting illicit messages. The importance of unimpeded correspondence with MPs outweighed the risk. By contrast, as regards correspondence with doctors, the prisoner's health was the concern and the immediate responsibility of the Prison Medical Service.

Since 22 May 2007 the applicant has been located in a Category B prison in Staffordshire. The interference in question had not denied the essence of the applicant’s Article 8 rights as it related to one correspondent only (the external medical specialist) and it confined the interference to a medically qualified reader (the prison medical officer) It was recognised that there was an inescapable risk of abuse, for example, if the applicant's prison life or treatment was made more difficult because of what he was observed to be writing. The withdrawal of monitoring had not only been considered but had been implemented until, upon reconsideration, monitoring had been resumed. The current conditions of imprisonment were clearly stated in Chapter 36.1 of PSO 1000.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 19840/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1921 and lives in Ascoli Piceno, Italy. He left the United Kingdom in 1982 following his retirement and moved to Italy with his wife. British citizens residing overseas for less than fifteen years are permitted to vote in parliamentary elections. The applicant does not meet the fifteen-year criterion and is therefore not entitled to vote. In particular, he was unable to voting in the general election of 5 May 2010. The application was rejected on the grounds that the applicant was not of age to vote and was therefore not eligible to do so. The case was dismissed on the basis that the application had been dismissed on a technicality.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 23883/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that their eviction from their flat following their refusal to remove a satellite dish resulted in violations of Articles 8 and 10. The President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The applicants were represented by Mr U. Isaksson, a lawyer practising in Stockholm, and by Mr P.-G. Nyström and Ms S. WikströM, lawyers of the Stockholm Tenants' Association.

The applicants, a married couple of Iraqi origin, were born in 1957 and 1963 respectively and live in Västerås. From 1 November 1999 they rented a flat in Rinkeby, a suburb of Stockholm. Rule 13 of the special provisions of the tenancy agreement stipulated the following: “The tenant undertakes not to erect, without specific permission, placards, signs, sunblinds, outdoor aerials and such like on the house” The agreement further stipulated, as a general condition, that the tenants were obliged to take proper care of the flat and to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice in the house.

Tenants' Association asked that a steel wire be fixed between the dish and the stand. The installation could be pulled back into the kitchen when not being used. The Board found that the fact that the new satellite installation extended through a window did not involve a breach of Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. With regard to the general obligation to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice in the house, the Board considered that the actual installation did not and could not damage the house. Also, the liability for damage to persons and property could not reasonably be incurred unless it were able to prevent it. In the applicants' case, they claimed that they were working on the possibility of installing broadband and internet access.

Landlord appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) The court held an oral hearing at which, inter alia, Mr Tornefelt gave evidence. It also made an inspection of the applicants' satellite installation. By a final decision of 20 December 2005, the court found that the applicants had disregarded their obligations as tenants to such a degree that the agreement should not be extended. They were given a respite until 31 March 2006 to move from the flat. The landlord had made a reasonable distinction between acceptable and unacceptable satellite installations and had submitted weighty reasons for prohibiting dishes mounted on the façade.

The applicants' three children had to change nursery and school and leave friends. As a consequence, the first applicant now had much longer and costlier trips to and from work. They have stated that, largely because of the scarcity of flats for rent in the Stockholm area, they were forced to move to Västerås, approximately 110 km west of Stockholm. They did not agree to do this, however, and instead moved on 1 June 2006. It noted, finally, that the applicants had been fully aware of the importance that the landlord attached to the issue of the placement of satellite dishes and of the consequences that could follow from a refusal to comply with the instructions.
rewrited_text: The case originated in an application (no. 23883/06) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants alleged that their eviction from their flat following their refusal to remove a satellite dish resulted in violations of Articles 8 and 10. The applicants were represented by Mr U. Isaksson, a lawyer practising in Stockholm. The Swedish Government was represented by their Agent, Mr C.-H Ehrenkrona, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. In April 2004, the landlord initiated proceedings before the Rent Review Board (hyresnämnden) in Stockholm against the applicants and some other tenants who had installed satellite dishes in the same house. The landlord sought execution of the notice of termination, claiming that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. The applicants dismantled the satellite dish and installed a new device by placing on the kitchen floor an iron stand from which an arm was mounted. The Rent Review Board gave a decision on 21 October 2004 finding in their favour. The landlord appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt) The court held an oral hearing at which, inter alia, Mr Tornefelt gave evidence. It also made an inspection of the applicants' satellite installation. By a final decision of 20 December 2005, the court found that the applicants had disregarded their obligations. The court found that the applicants' dish was virtually always positioned outside the kitchen window and thus constituted a permanent installation. It concluded, contrary to the findings of the Rent Review Board, that its placement breached Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. The applicants had been fully aware of the importance that the landlord attached to the issue of the placement of satellite dishes and of the consequences that could follow from a refusal to comply with the landlord's instructions in this respect.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 32848/06) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. By a decision of 9 October 2007 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant submitted his claims for just satisfaction. The Government made their comments on that matter. The Court ruled that the application was admissible and that the Government's comments on the matter were not relevant. The case was decided in favour of the applicant, and the decision was upheld by the Court.

The applicant was born in 1958 and lives in Charlottenlund. He was part owner of a private limited stockbrokers company. He learnt that the tax authorities were about to check the company’s accounts for the years 1989 to 1992. On 17 June 1996, the Copenhagen City Court (Københavns Byret – hereafter ‘the City Court’) granted the police a warrant to search the premises of the applicant and those of the company. On 2 July 1996 the search was carried out by the police. From July 1996 to February 1998 various investigative steps were taken, also relating to five co-accused in the case.

The applicant was charged on forty-four counts out of a total of fifty-nine, committed between 26 June and 3 November 1992. The indictment related to eighty different companies and six banks in Denmark and abroad. The applicant was sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. In addition, the sum of DKK 3,600,000 was seized, and he was deprived for an indefinite period of the right to establish a private limited company or a company or an association requiring public approval. The City Court found no reason to criticise the prosecution’s decision to join the criminal proceedings against the [applicant and the five co‑accused]. The co-accused were also convicted.

The City Court finds no violation of Article 6 of the Convention, although there were longer periods of inactivity during one part of the case. The complexity of the acts carried out by [the applicant and the five co-accused] partly when buying and “stripping” the companies for assets, partly when writing off projects abroad, necessitated an investigation of an extraordinary scope. The High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the City Court’s judgment on 28 September 2004. The Court records comprised 861 pages. The closing speeches were held over ten days in April, May, and June 2004. In February and March 2004 the appeal hearings had to be postponed because a co-defendant fell ill.

The appeal proceedings were scheduled and carried out without any unreasonable delay. The applicant and the co‑defendants requested that the Leave to Appeal Board (Procesbevillingsnævnet) grant them leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) Three of the defendants stated in their petitions that they would submit supplementary comments, which were received on 17 December 2004. In January 2005 the cases were sent to the prosecution, which gave its opinion on 29 March 2005. At a meeting on 5 August 2005 the Leave To Appeal Board decided to refuse the requests. Thereafter, due to an error, nothing happened in the case until 2 May 2006, when the police telephoned the leave board and drew attention to the case.

background_knowledge: The case originated in two applications (nos. 8319/07 and 11449/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that if returned to Somalia they would be at real risk of ill-treatment contrary to Article 3 and/or a violation of Article 2. They also complained that their removal would disproportionately interfere with their rights under Article 8. At the Government’s request the cases were adjourned on 7 October 2008 pending the decision of the Court of Appeal in HH (Somalia), AM (S Somalia) and MA (Somalia) v Secretary of State for the Home Department.

The first applicant, Mr Abdisamad Adow Sufi, is a Somali national who was born in 1987 and is currently in detention in an Immigration Detention Centre in West Drayton. On 3 October 2003 he claimed asylum on the ground that as a member of the Reer-Hamar, a sub-clan of the minority Ahansi clan, he had been subjected to persecution by Hawiye militia. On 15 April 2005 the Secretary of State for the Home Department refused the first applicant’s asylum application, finding, inter alia, that the fact he had remained in Somalia until 2003 undermined his claim to be a minority clan. On 16 May 2005 he appealed against the refusal of the application on both asylum and human rights grounds, namely Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention. On 29 June 2005 both the asylum appeal and the human rights appeal were dismissed by an Adjudicator who found that his account of what had happened to him in Somalia was not credible.

The second applicant, Mr Abdiaziz Ibrahim Elmi, is a Somali national who was born in 1969 and is currently detained in an Immigration Detention Centre. His father, a high-ranking officer in the army during the Barré regime, was appointed to the Somali Embassy in London as a military attaché in 1988. On 1 March 1989 his father died. On 26 April 1989 the second applicant made an application for asylum based on his father’s position in the Somali army and the beginning of the civil war in Somalia. On 31 October 1989 he was recognised as a refugee and granted leave to remain until 31 October 1993. On 7 January 1994 he was granted Indefinite Leave to Remain in the United Kingdom.

The second applicant was convicted of supplying class A drugs (cocaine and heroin) and was sentenced to 42 months’ imprisonment. On 21 June 2006 a decision was made to issue a deportation order by virtue of section 3(5) of the Immigration Act 1971. He accepted that he was a drug addict but submitted that he did not constitute a danger to the community because he had made efforts to overcome his addiction and had recognised his past wrongdoings. The Secretary of State for the Home Department found that he had failed to demonstrate that he would not constitute such a danger. In respect of his rights under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention, the Secretary of. State found that even though he had been living in the United Kingdom and could be identified as such he would. not be at risk on return to Somalia as he was. a member of the Isaaq, a majority clan.

A deportation order against the second applicant was signed on 8 January 2007 and on 6 March 2007 he was served with removal directions. On 3 March 2008 he was convicted of possession of a Class A controlled drug with intent to supply and was sentenced to eighteen months’ imprisonment. On 8 July 2010 he was again charged with possession of the same drug. A hearing has not yet taken place. Finally, the AIT noted that the sale of drugs posed a danger to the community and there was a real likelihood of the second applicants re‑offending. The second applicant requested, and was granted, interim measures to prevent his removal before his application was considered by the Court.

Under current UK law, the state pension age is 65 for men and 60 for women. A woman of 60 years or more who continued to work would not be needed to pay any NICs.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 41534/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The case concerned proceedings before his Commanding Officer (“CO”) The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. By a decision of 15 November 2005, a Chamber of the Fourth Section of the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The Government, but not the applicant, filed further written observations in the case.

The applicant was born in 1973 and lived in Surrey. He was a soldier serving as a Private with the Grenadier Guards of the British Army, stationed at Alexandra Barracks in Northern Ireland. On the evening of 19 December 1997 the applicant was talking with an officer, Captain J, in the foyer of the cookhouse at the barracks. There followed an exchange of words between the applicant and a non-commissioned officer, Sergeant H, who subsequently ordered the applicant locked up overnight. The applicant was released the following morning and went to the medical centre. He submitted that his examination established that he had not had a nose bleed the night before.

The applicant claimed that Corporal G had been directed not to give evidence in support of his case. The Government argued that it was routine for witnesses to be called into the Regimental Sergeant Major’s office so that the procedure to be followed at the hearing could be explained. The hearing lasted approximately ten minutes. The applicant was required to stand to attention throughout the hearing and was permitted to speak only when invited to do so by the CO. The CO asked the applicant if he admitted the offence described and the applicant pleaded not guilty. The application was dismissed on appeal and the case against the applicant was dismissed. The case was dismissed and the appeal was upheld.

The applicant served his sentence in a locked cell in the battalion guardroom. Corporal G did not give evidence. The company commander, who was present by this time, said that the applicant was a satisfactory member of his company. The CO then said that he found the applicant guilty and sentenced him to seven days' detention and seven days’ associated loss of pay. The applicant said he would accept the CO’s award and serve the sentence in the guardroom, where he was locked in a cell with no food or water. The application was rejected by the court-martial judge, who said the applicant had been a 'satisfactory' member of the company.

The applicant claimed that he then went to the medical centre and asked for a record of his examination establishing that he had not had a nose bleed on the night in question. He claimed that staff at the medical center refused to provide the record and the Government disputed this. The hearing lasted approximately ten minutes. The applicant was required to stand to attention throughout the hearing and was permitted to speak only when invited to do so by the CO. An officer appointed to look after the applicant’s interests, whose identity remained unknown to the applicant and with whom he had not discussed his case, did not speak at any point during the hearing. The applicant served his sentence in a locked cell in the battalion guardroom.

background_knowledge: The case originated in an application (no. 28212/95) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights on 3 August 1995. The applicants alleged that they had not had available to them a procedure by which they could challenge the lawfulness of their continued detention. The application was declared admissible by the Commission on 23 October 1997 and transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section.

The first applicant, Mr Patrick Benjamin, was sentenced to life imprisonment for rape in 1983. His tariff period (the minimum period of detention satisfying the requirements of retribution and deterrence) was set at six years and expired in April 1989. His time in prison was characterised by periods of thought disorder, delusions and behavioural problems and the Secretary of State decided that he was in need of care and treatment in a secure hospital. In August 1989, he was made the subject of a transfer direction and a restriction order under, respectively, sections 47 and 49 of the Mental Health Act 1983 (the 1983 Act) and transferred to Broadmoor Special Hospital. In April 1994, the first applicant was transferred to Bracton Clinic Regional Secure Unit. In January 2001, the MHR Tribunal recommended his discharge.

In October 1992, the second applicant was transferred to Rampton Special Hospital under sections 47 and 49 of the 1983 Act. In June 1993, following consultation with the trial judge and the Lord Chief Justice, the Secretary of State decided that he should be regarded as a ‘technical lifer’ In July 1996 the MHR Tribunal found that they were not satisfied that he no longer required treatment in hospital for mental illness. His case was reviewed most recently on 13 June 2000 when the Tribunal again did not recommend discharge. the applicant returned to prison and there were several other transfers to and from hospital in subsequent years. The applicants were informed by letter of 18 May 1995 that the House of Lords had refused leave to appeal.
